newsitem.title: MEXICO: Smog woes descend on Mexico's second city.
newsitem.headline: Smog woes descend on Mexico's second city.

text.p: Guadalajara, Mexico's second biggest city, is beginning to suffer from the same smog woes that afflict the nation's capital, one of the most polluted cities in the world, experts say.
For the first time ozone levels have risen above levels considered safe for human health, and the coming winter is expected to worsen the situation.
"Only Mexico City and now Guadalajara have shown such high levels of contamination in this country," Jose Zaragoza Avila of the National Ecology Institute told Reuters.
Guadalajara residents began to get seriously worried last week when some areas of the city registered ozone levels above 250 Imecas.
An ozone level above 100 Imecas is considered bad for human beings, giving rise to respiratory and lung complaints.
"Pollution here has grown apace with industrial growth and development," said Zaragoza, who monitors air quality in the city.
The city's top ecology official, Jorge Sierra, said about "2,000 tonnes a day of pollution are being generated and going into the atmosphere".
"The situation of air quality in the urban area of Guadalajara is beginning to show an unfavourable tendency, above all in the cold months," he told a recent news conference.
The top ecology official in the state of Jalisco, of which Guadalajara is the capital, said city authorities were likely to have to order anti-smog measures this winter.
"There is no doubt that we would have to implement Phase One again," said Ramon Gonzalez, predicting more periods of what Mexican authorities call "environmental contingency", when smog levels soar.

On October 17 authorities ordered Phase One of the city's anti-smog plan after levels hit 264 Imecas. Phase One consists of halting tarring of roads and activity at brickworks, cutting use of government vehicles by half and taking special measures to speed up traffic flow.
On Tuesday ozone levels hit 270 Imecas in some parts of Guadalajara, but Phase One was only partly implemented.
Unlike Mexico City, Guadalajara does not ban vehicles from the roads one day a week in an attempt to reduce smog, though such measures are being studied.
"In Guadalajara, as in Mexico City, most of the pollution emissions come from vehicles, and something must be done about it," said Alejandro Calvillo, Greenpeace energy coordinator in Mexico.
